findings.title: Redirect resolution loop limit silently reduced 10000 -> 1000
findings.body: The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

findings.title: Eviction silently drops spans from oversized segments without logging
findings.body: Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

findings.title: `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

findings.title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors
findings.body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

findings.title: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` may AttributeError if member is None
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` (line 71) unconditionally accesses `.member.has_global_access` whenever the requester is not a superuser. If `organization_context.member` is None for any path that reaches this endpoint (e.g., a service user or a context shape returned for non-members of the org being queried), the request will raise `AttributeError` and return a 500. The original code never touched `organization_context.member`, so this PR introduces the regression. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access` (or equivalent), or move the check inside the `optimized_pagination` branch where it is actually consumed.

findings.title: Privileged pagination feature is gated by a client-controlled query parameter
findings.body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` (line 70) lets any requester who is also a superuser (or has global access) flip on `enable_advanced_features=True` for that single request. Privileged behavior is typically gated by server-side configuration or user attributes, not a query parameter, because query-parameter gating leaves no audit trail and is trivially selectable. The 'feature' itself just re-enables Django's native negative-offset slicing that the BasePaginator change (line 182 in paginator.py) just removed. Either move the toggle behind a server-side feature flag/setting, or drop it — the parameter offers no functional benefit beyond Django's existing behavior.

findings.title: No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior
findings.body: The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

findings.title: No tests cover the redirect-loop limit change (10000 -> 1000) or the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path
findings.body: Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

findings.title: `cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError
findings.body: Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

findings.title: Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't
findings.body: Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. Either delete the comment or move the explanatory text to the place that actually implements the feature.
